record.paper_title: Ductile-to-brittle transition and yielding in soft amorphous materials: perspectives and open questions
record.original_question: How should computational models of epithelial and tissue mechanics, including Potts, Voronoi, and vertex models, incorporate characteristic time scales, critical shear rates, rearrangement domains, difficult-to-define viscosity, possible breakdown of two-dimensional monolayer assumptions, substrate friction, cell-cell dissipation, cell-substrate adhesion, matrix rigidity, organoid or tumor-spheroid environments, and molecular mechanochemical sensitivity?

evidence.quote: These experiments also showed that a viscosity could be difficult to define and measure in this context. All these different ingredients still remain to be incorporated into vertex models. Moreover, these models are, for now, mainly used for describing cell monolayers that are considered two-dimensional systems. Nevertheless, it is not clear whether such a 2D assumption is always appropriate.

More generally , including properly the effects of boundary conditions, such as the differential role of substrate friction and pair dissipation between cells, is crucial to describe the dynamics of deforming tissues.
This discovery raises intriguing questions about the interplay between boundary conditions and the dynamics of biological systems.

artifact.status_search_result: This is a broad modeling and research-program question rather than a single sharply formulated conjecture. No comprehensive vertex/Voronoi/Potts model that simultaneously incorporates all the listed ingredients (3D effects, substrate friction vs. cell–cell dissipation, matrix rigidity, organoid geometry, mechanochemical feedback, well-defined viscosity and critical shear rate) is known; recent literature continues to address these features piecemeal. The question is therefore open as a unified problem.
